Artificial intelligence changes how we write software and run our businesses. Today, frontier AI models manage complex workflows, analyze data, and operate digital tools. Following the release of the flagship GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI expanded its model family. On September 23, 2026, the company officially launched GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

results.title: New Anthropic, OpenAI models make same promise: A little more for a lot less money
results.content:
It may not be obvious what those names mean, so here’s the quick rundown. Astra is the most aggressively powerful (and pricey) model, meant for heavy-duty coding, research, and so on. Sol is a capable but more efficient and affordable alternative—meant to be the sort of daily driver for tasks like that. Terra is the balanced, general-use model. And Luna is the fast, cheap option. ### The correct interpretation

“Astra compared to GPT-5.6 Sol” currently means comparing a documented model with a documented frontier-development program—not two equally specified commercial models. A defensible comparison should therefore mark Astra’s context window, modalities, tools, pricing, token consumption, cybersecurity scores, and release status as unknown, rather than inferring them from the Astra name or roadmap language.

## Is Astra more token-efficient than GPT-5.6 Sol? [...] A credible GPT-6 Astra vs GPT-5.6 Sol comparison can now evaluate two released models rather than comparing a deployable model with a development roadmap.

OpenAI’s official materials establish these relevant facts: [...] The decisive difference is documented product availability. OpenAI’s API documentation identifies GPT-5.6 Sol as a flagship model in the GPT-5.6 family, while the supplied Astra publication documents a direction for critical capabilities and frontier safeguards rather than complete product specifications. Consequently, an evidence-based OpenAI Astra comparison must distinguish verified Sol features from Astra goals and unknowns.

results.title: GPT-6 Astra, Looped Transformers, and Hidden Reasoning
results.content:
However, I think it’s highly likely that GPT-6 Astra uses looped transformer aspects. First, there is the reporting mentioned above. Second, it’s a technique that has shown promise in past studies (as discussed earlier), so why not? Third, OpenAI’s chief scientist said the following.

> [...] The depth of the computation graph for our present frontier models, including Astra, is within a factor of two of GPT-4. [...] [...] > I want to prevent a race into unmonitorability kicked off by confused reporting. The depth of the computation graph for our present frontier models, including Astra, is within a factor of two of GPT-4. OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models. We deeply care about this technique, as it can give us a view into how model alignment generalizes from its training distribution. I do think it is fragile and unfortunately trending in [...] So, why would we do this looping in general? This is essentially an alternative to just making the model bigger by adding more transformer blocks.

So, for instance, a model that uses 22 transformer blocks twice has roughly half as many (transformer-block) parameters compared to a model with 44 conventional blocks.

results.title: OpenAI model release dates: o3, GPT-5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, Sol and Luna in order · Think Facility
results.content:
GPT-6 kept two of those names and moved one of them. Astra is the new top, and the models page now says to use it if you're "not sure where to start". GPT-6 Sol is the middle model, there to "balance intelligence and cost", which is the job Terra had. Luna is still the cheap one. There's no GPT-6 Terra on the page at all. [...] ## Astra, Sol, Terra, Luna: which GPT is which

This is the part that confused me. In July, OpenAI stopped using plain version numbers and gave the GPT-5.6 family three names: Sol "for frontier capability", Terra "for a balance of intelligence and cost" and Luna "for efficient, high-volume workloads". Sol was the top. [...] Two columns of tiers. GPT-5.6 from July 9 has Sol on top, Terra in the middle and Luna at the bottom. GPT-6 from September has Astra on top, marked new, Sol in the middle and Luna at the bottom. An arrow carries Sol from the top tier down to the middle, Luna stays level, and Terra's line ends at a cross marked no GPT-6 Terra.

Sol moved down a tier between generations, and Terra didn't come along.

results.title: GPT models explained: ChatGPT models from GPT-1 to GPT-6.1
results.content:
These aren’t four quality settings on the same model. They are distinct models designed to occupy different points on the capability, speed and cost curve. Astra is the frontier model for the hardest work. Sol carries near-Astra capability for complex professional work and coding. Terra is the balanced tier for everyday and computer-use work, and Luna is the efficient tier for cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads. [...] The latest GPT models are GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s flagship released in September 2026, and two GPT-6.1 point releases: GPT-6.1 Sol (September 29) and GPT-6.1 Terra (October 26). GPT-6 Luna is the low-cost tier. In ChatGPT, paid plans chat with GPT-6 Sol, the Pro option uses Astra, and Free and Go users get GPT-6 Luna.

## What is GPT? [...] As of late October 2026, the GPT lineup has four tiers across two version numbers. Which one you get depends on where you use it: the ChatGPT Chat tab, ChatGPT Work, Codex or the API.
